topics.label: Introduction and lecture objectives
topics.groupedBecause: This opening frames the lecture within the cancer course and sets out its learning objectives.

topics.label: Genetic evolution and susceptibility to cancer
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how accumulating mutations can produce cancer when cellular susceptibility and the surrounding microenvironment permit clonal growth.

topics.label: Environmental cancer risk and the bad luck hypothesis
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine the contribution of environmental exposures to cancer risk and the evidence against interpreting cancer as simply unavoidable bad luck.

topics.label: Infectious agents in cancer development
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how infections can drive carcinogenesis, with Burkitt lymphoma illustrating the interaction between pathogens and cellular mutations.

topics.label: Environmental carcinogens and mechanisms of DNA damage
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how environmental carcinogens damage DNA, showing how their mutagenic effects depend on chemical reactivity and biological processing.

topics.label: Tumour promotion and two-stage carcinogenesis
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics distinguish tumour promotion from mutation initiation by explaining how growth-permissive conditions enable previously initiated cells to form tumours.

topics.label: Developmental and tissue-specific susceptibility to carcinogens
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how the biological context of exposure determines susceptibility to carcinogenesis and conclude the preceding account of carcinogenic mechanisms.

topics.label: Methods for assessing carcinogenicity and their limitations
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine how evidence of carcinogenicity is obtained and why the available approaches cannot fully establish human cancer risk on their own.

topics.label: Closing summary and risk–benefit decisions
topics.groupedBecause: This closing brings the lecture's conclusions together around the difficulty of assessing carcinogenic risk and weighing it against benefits.
